extracted.intended_audience: general readers; writers and readers interested in flash/microfiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for composing and understanding flash fiction (very short fiction), including recognized word‑count varieties, salient literary qualities, and publication venues. Useful for writers preparing microfiction and readers/editors evaluating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity with character and plot development
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is a brief fictional narrative that still offers character and plot development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even within extreme brevity the piece should provide some sense of character and a development of events (plot) rather than being merely a vignette or image. Examples in the article (historical and contemporary practitioners) illustrate how authors compress development into very short forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to hint at or imply a larger story (hint fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction possesses a unique literary quality in its ability to hint at or imply a larger story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good flash often suggests backstory, consequences, or a wider context beyond the few words on the page; classic examples and references (e.g., the six‑word story tradition, hint fiction anthologies) show how implication/subtext does much of the narrative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties defined by word count / formal constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties are sometimes defined by word count, including the six‑word story, the 280‑character story ('twitterature'), the 'dribble'/'minisaga' (50 words), and the 'drabble'/'microfiction' (100 words).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions and limits vary by venue and tradition: contests have ranged (e.g., Jerome Stern's contest under 250 words; some contests/journals allow up to 500). When writing or submitting, check the specific word/character limits of the target publication or contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of language — 'every word counts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision and economy are central: every word must serve purpose and contribute to meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should eliminate filler and choose words that carry weight (denotation, connotation, rhythm). The article cites contest coverage noting that 'every word counts' — a practical editorial rule when composing flash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensed tone — intensity, urgency, and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is often described as 'intense, urgent and a little explosive' — a condensed emotional or thematic impact is typical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concentrated affect or a sharp twist/surprise. Tone and emotional effect should be achieved without extended build‑up; the piece's brevity should amplify rather than dilute its impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishability: appropriate venues and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction is commonly published in both dedicated print journals and online journals; the internet has expanded outlets and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target publications that accept very short forms (examples: Flash: The International Short‑Short Story Magazine; online venues like Wigleaf, SmokeLong Quarterly, Tin House's Flash features, The New Yorker online series). Be aware that venues may have different formatting or length expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility of form and cultural traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Flash fiction draws on many traditions (fable, parable, koan, anecdote) and may adopt a wide range of cultural and formal approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers may borrow strategies from parables, zen koans, aphorisms, or other brief narrative traditions to achieve compression and meaning; awareness of these antecedents can inform choices about voice, structure, and rhetorical effect.
